per_ply.human_comment:
This game was published only in 1900, in the chess column of the
newspaper "Niva", with a curious introduction by Chigorin. He wrote:
"Sometimes may happen that a chess game is repeated from the first move to the
last one. It is possible when an unexperienced player in the opening play some
natural- and good-looking move. Indeed such moves drive him to a defeat. One
of such games will be now shown to you. The following opening is very common
in amateur practice, and my opponent, an enthusiastic amateur has played it
four times against me." Chigorin does not tell us if there was a fifth time
where his opponent, convinced by the previous four kicks, found the right
continuation. I think this player should be remembered as "Knorr the
tenacious".
per_ply.system_comment: The game opens as a King's Pawn Game (B00).
The game transposes into the King's Knight Opening (C40).
The game transposes into the Italian Game (C50).
The game transposes into the Giuoco Pianissimo: 4.d3 Nf6 5.O-O (C50).
This is the last book move of the Giuoco Pianissimo: 4.d3 Nf6 5.O-O d6 (C50); both sides are on their own from here.

per_ply.system_comment: White missed the chance to target the bishop on c5 and the potential to leave Black's pieces more passive. Instead, 9.Nxg5 throws away the advantage and hands Black a slight advantage (+0.28 → -0.58, Stockfish:16), as [pv:Nxg5 h4 Nxf7 Qe7 Nxh8] immediately weakens Black's pawn structure with doubled, isolated, and backward pawns, while the line could yield a passed pawn on g2. b4 leads to a slight advantage for White [pv:b4 Bb6 h4 g4 Ng5].

The most accurate move maintains Black's advantage (-0.50, Stockfish:16), as [pv:h4 Nxf7 Qe7 Nxh8 hxg3] preserves Black's edge while accepting that, deeper in the line, White may win the exchange. By contrast, 9...Bg4 was clearly weaker, leading to a slight advantage for White with [pv:Bg4 Qd2 h4 Nxf7 Qe7], since it immediately targets the queen on d1 yet fails to hold Black's advantage.

Black missed the chance to keep the king safe with Qe7. Instead, 10...hxg3 immediately targets the queen on d1 and could leave White's king under pressure along [pv:hxg3 Nxd8 Bg4 Qe1 Nd4], yet it lets the advantage slip away to equality (-0.48 → +0.24, Stockfish:16). Qe7 leads to a slight advantage for Black [pv:Qe7 b4 Bb6 Nxh8 hxg3].

White's most accurate move holds the balance (+0.23, Stockfish:16), as [pv:Nxd8 Bg4 Qd2 Nd4 Ne6] immediately targets the knight on c6. Nxh8 was a roughly comparable option that also leads to equality with [pv:Nxh8 Bxf2+ Kh1 Qe7 Rxf2], winning the exchange on the spot and, deeper in that line, potentially leaving Black without the bishop-pair edge—but keeping the c6 knight under pressure is the sharper way to maintain the equilibrium, and Black soon answers with...Nd4 to hold the balance.

Black's most accurate move holds the balance (+0.11, Stockfish:16), with [pv:Nd4 Ne6] the clearest way to keep the game level. Rxd8 would have been clearly weaker, handing White a winning advantage [pv:Rxd8 Nc3 Kd7 Qg5 Bxf2+]: Black's king would be safe at once, but pawn-structure improvements would only emerge later in the line.

White still holds a queen, knight, and pawn for a bishop—a useful material edge—but 13.Nc3 is punished by Nf3+, which leads to forced mate for Black (#7 for Black, Stockfish:16) after [pv:Nc3 Nf3+ gxf3 Bxf3 Bf7+], as Black adds another piece to the kingside attack. White missed the chance to reach equality with 13.Nxb7, which leads to equality via [pv:Nxb7 Ne2+ Qxe2 Bxe2 Bb5+], keeping a queen and three pawns for a bishop while Black's pawn structure is now weaker with doubled, isolated, and backward pawns.

Black's Nf3+ adds another piece to the kingside attack, stepping up pressure toward White's king. The sequence [pv:Nf3+ gxf3 Bxf3 Bf7+ Kxd8] may leave Black two pieces for a pawn—a material surplus that usually keeps an attack rolling. This move leads to forced mate for Black (#6 for Black, Stockfish:16), and after 14.gxf3 the same forcing threat remains on the table.

White's 14.gxf3 leads to forced mate for Black (#6 for Black, Stockfish:16), as [pv:gxf3 Bxf3 Bf7+ Kxd8 Qh6] shows: after...Bxf3, White's Bf7+ is met by...Kxd8, and...Qh6 finishes the mating attack with no way out. Black went on to win the game.
